title: Yeast cell size in different growth media
stem: Yeast cells were grown for 24 hours in three liquid media. Samples were photographed with a light microscope and the image diameter of 50 cells per medium was measured on prints enlarged to a magnification of ×4000.

data.caption: Mean image diameter of yeast cells at ×4000 (n = 50 per medium)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean actual diameter of yeast cells grown in 2 % glucose. Give your answer in µm.
markscheme: conversion: 22.0 mm = 22 000 µm
22 000 / 4000 = 5.5 µm (unit required)
parts.notes: Award 1 mark for 0.0055 mm or for a correct method with a unit-conversion error.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage difference in mean cell diameter between cells grown in 2 % ethanol and cells grown in 2 % glucose, relative to 2 % glucose.
markscheme: −36.4 % / 36 % smaller (sign or 'smaller/decrease' required)
parts.notes: Allow working with actual diameters (3.5 µm and 5.5 µm) as the ratio is the same.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the standard deviations, deduce whether the difference in mean diameter between cells grown in 0.5 % glucose and cells grown in 2 % ethanol is likely to be significant.
markscheme: ranges of mean ± 1 SD: 0.5 % glucose 13.9–18.1 mm; ethanol 10.5–17.5 mm
the ranges overlap (considerably)
so the difference is unlikely to be significant / cannot conclude it is significant (without a statistical test)
ethanol has the larger SD so cell size is more variable in ethanol
parts.notes: Do not award a conclusion of 'significant' without reference to the SD values.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one reason why yeast cells grown in 2 % glucose were larger than cells in the other media.
markscheme: glucose is an abundant/readily used energy source / respiratory substrate
more ATP available for biosynthesis / for synthesis of proteins/membranes/organelles
cells grow larger before dividing / more cytoplasm produced
ethanol is a poorer energy source / is toxic at higher concentration / damages membranes
lower glucose concentration limits growth rate
parts.notes: Accept any reasoned link between energy supply and growth, OWTTE.

title: Mitochondrial sequences of cave beetles
stem: A 1200 base-pair section of a mitochondrial gene was sequenced from four species of cave beetle (W, X, Y and Z) living in neighbouring cave systems. The number of base differences between each pair of species is shown.

data.caption: Pairwise base differences in a 1200 bp mitochondrial gene sequence

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage sequence difference between species W and Y.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Assuming this gene diverges at 2.0 % per million years, estimate how long ago species W and X shared a common ancestor.
markscheme: percentage difference W – X = 18 / 1200 × 100 = 1.5 %
1.5 / 2.0 = 0.75 million years / 750 000 years
parts.notes: ECF for an incorrect percentage correctly divided by 2.0.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce the relationships between the four species, as they would appear on a cladogram.
markscheme: W and X form one clade / are most closely related (fewest differences, 18)
Y and Z form a second clade (24 differences)
the two clades (W+X and Y+Z) diverged earliest / share a more distant common ancestor (64–70 differences)
W and X diverged more recently than Y and Z

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Evaluate the use of a molecular clock based on this gene for dating the divergence of these species.
markscheme: strength: mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate so differences give an approximate time
strength: objective / quantitative / independent of morphology (which may show convergent evolution in caves)
limitation: mutation rate may differ between lineages / genes / over time
limitation: rate of 2.0 % per million years is an assumption that needs calibration (e.g. with fossils / dated geological events)
limitation: only one gene / short sequence used / mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally only
limitation: multiple mutations at the same site (back mutation) can cause underestimation of older divergences
parts.notes: At least one strength and one limitation for full marks.

title: Snail shells and an invasive crab
stem: A shore crab that crushes snail shells arrived on a coastline in 2008 and spread along it. Shell thickness of an intertidal snail was measured at three sites in 2005 and again in 2020 (n = 40 snails per site each year).

data.caption: Mean shell thickness of snails at three sites

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in mean shell thickness at site 2 between 2005 and 2020.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean rate of change in shell thickness at site 2 between 2005 and 2020, stating the unit.
markscheme: 0.26 mm / 15 years = 0.017 mm year⁻¹ (unit required)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the changes in shell thickness at sites 2 and 3.
markscheme: both sites show an increase in mean thickness
greater increase at site 2 (0.26 mm) than site 3 (0.14 mm)
similar starting thickness in 2005 at both sites (0.80 and 0.81 mm)
site 2 had crabs for longer (12 years vs 6 years)
parts.notes: Quoted values are needed for a comparison of magnitude.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Evaluate the hypothesis that predation by the crab has caused natural selection for thicker shells.
markscheme: support: no (meaningful) change at site 1 without crabs (0.82 to 0.84 mm)
support: increase is greater where crabs have been present longer / dose–response with time
support: thicker shells less likely to be crushed so those snails survive and reproduce more
limitation: thickening could be phenotypic plasticity (snails grow thicker shells when crabs are detected) rather than genetic change
limitation: only three sites / no replication of sites / correlation does not prove causation
limitation: other factors may differ between sites, e.g. water temperature / calcium availability / snail age
limitation: no SD given for 2005 so significance of change cannot be judged
parts.notes: At least one supporting and one limiting point for full marks.

title: One-step growth of a bacteriophage
stem: A culture of bacteria was mixed with a bacteriophage so that each infected cell received one phage; unattached phages were then removed. At intervals, samples were plated to count plaque-forming units (PFU). Before lysis, each infected cell produces one plaque. Means of three plates are shown.

data.caption: Mean count of plaque-forming units after infection (n = 3)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the time interval during which lysis of infected cells began.
markscheme: between 20 and 30 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of phages released per infected cell (burst size).
markscheme: plateau value / initial infected cells: 200 / 2.0 (allow 190–202 / 2.0)
≈ 100 phages per cell

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the changes in PFU between 0 and 40 minutes with reference to the lytic cycle.
markscheme: 0–20 min no increase as phage DNA/RNA is inside host cells / latent period
phage genes are transcribed/translated using host ribosomes/enzymes/ATP
phage nucleic acid is replicated and new capsid proteins are made
new phage particles are assembled inside the cell
from 20–30 min host cells lyse / burst releasing many new phages, so PFU rise sharply
lysis is not simultaneous in all cells so the rise continues to 40 min

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest why the PFU count does not increase further after 50 minutes.
markscheme: all infected cells have lysed / no further infected cells
released phages could not infect new hosts (uninfected cells removed / too dilute / sampling stopped infection)

title: Base composition and nucleic acid structure
stem: Analysis of double-stranded DNA from a soil bacterium showed that 22 % of the bases were adenine.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of bases in this DNA that are guanine.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish between the structure of DNA and RNA.
markscheme: DNA contains deoxyribose whereas RNA contains ribose
DNA contains thymine whereas RNA contains uracil
DNA is (usually) double-stranded whereas RNA is (usually) single-stranded
DNA forms a double helix whereas RNA does not
DNA molecules are (usually) much longer than RNA molecules
parts.notes: Each point must state both sides of the difference; a list of DNA features alone scores 0.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how complementary base pairing allows DNA to be copied accurately.
markscheme: A pairs only with T and C pairs only with G
pairing is by hydrogen bonds between bases (2 between A–T, 3 between C–G)
pairing depends on shape and hydrogen-bonding pattern of the bases / purine pairs with pyrimidine
each strand acts as a template for a new strand
so the sequence of the new strand is determined by the template / new molecules are identical to the original
semi-conservative replication: each new molecule keeps one original strand

title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
stem: All living organisms are composed of cells, but cell structure differs between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State two structures found in all cells.
markscheme: plasma / cell membrane
cytoplasm
ribosomes
DNA / genetic material

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
markscheme: similarity: both have plasma membrane / cytoplasm / ribosomes / DNA
prokaryotes have no nucleus / DNA in nucleoid whereas eukaryotes have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope
prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes whereas eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm
prokaryotic DNA is circular / naked whereas eukaryotic DNA is linear and associated with histones
prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles / eukaryotes have mitochondria, ER, Golgi etc.
prokaryotes may have plasmids; eukaryotes rarely do
prokaryotic cells are (usually) much smaller
parts.notes: For full marks at least one similarity and one difference are needed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Outline evidence that mitochondria originated by endosymbiosis.
markscheme: mitochondria have a double membrane / inner membrane resembling a prokaryote membrane
they contain their own circular / naked DNA
they have 70S ribosomes
they divide by binary fission / are not made by the cell from scratch
they are similar in size to bacteria
their DNA / ribosomal RNA sequences are closely related to those of (alpha-proteo)bacteria
they are sensitive to some antibiotics that affect bacteria

title: Species and the biodiversity crisis
stem: Conservation programmes aim to protect species, but deciding what counts as a species is not always straightforward.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the biological species concept and one difficulty in applying it.
markscheme: a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
difficulty: cannot be applied to asexually reproducing organisms / bacteria
difficulty: cannot test interbreeding of extinct/fossil species
difficulty: some distinct species hybridize and produce fertile offspring
difficulty: populations that are geographically separated cannot be tested / ring species

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe three causes of the current loss of biodiversity.
markscheme: habitat destruction / land-use change e.g. deforestation for agriculture
overexploitation e.g. overfishing / hunting / poaching
pollution e.g. eutrophication / pesticides / plastics
invasive alien species that outcompete / prey on native species
climate change altering habitats faster than species can adapt / migrate
spread of pathogens / disease
parts.notes: Each cause needs a brief description or example, not just a single word.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish between in situ and ex situ conservation.
markscheme: in situ: protecting species in their natural habitat e.g. nature reserves / national parks
ex situ: protecting species outside their natural habitat e.g. zoos / botanic gardens / seed banks
in situ conserves the whole ecosystem and interactions; ex situ only the target species
ex situ allows captive breeding / storage of genetic material for later reintroduction

title: Water as the medium of life
stem: Water has properties that make it essential for living organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
markscheme: oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen
so electrons in O–H covalent bonds are shared unequally
water molecule is polar: oxygen partially negative (δ−), hydrogens partially positive (δ+)
molecule is bent / V-shaped so charges do not cancel
hydrogen bond is an attraction between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another
hydrogen bonds are weak individually but numerous / constantly forming and breaking
each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline how cohesion and adhesion of water are important to living organisms.
markscheme: cohesion: water molecules stick to each other due to hydrogen bonds
cohesion allows water to be pulled up xylem in continuous columns under tension
cohesion causes surface tension, supporting small organisms on water surfaces
adhesion: water molecules are attracted to other polar / charged surfaces
adhesion to cellulose in xylem walls / capillary action helps water rise
adhesion allows water to move through cell walls / soil pores by capillary action

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how the physical and solvent properties of water affect organisms that live in water and the transport of substances in organisms.
markscheme: high specific heat capacity: much energy needed to change temperature
so aquatic habitats have stable temperatures / buffer organisms against change
high latent heat of vaporization allows cooling by sweating / transpiration
thermal conductivity of water is high so aquatic animals lose heat quickly / need insulation e.g. blubber
water is buoyant / dense so supports organisms and reduces need for skeletal support
water is more viscous than air so aquatic animals need streamlined bodies to reduce drag
ice is less dense than liquid water so floats and insulates water below / organisms survive under ice
water is a solvent for polar / charged (hydrophilic) substances
so glucose / amino acids / ions dissolve and are transported in blood plasma / phloem / xylem
non-polar substances (e.g. lipids / cholesterol) are insoluble so must be carried in lipoproteins
oxygen has low solubility so is carried by haemoglobin
metabolic reactions occur in solution in cytoplasm
parts.notes: Award marks for linking a property to its biological consequence; a bare list of properties scores at most 2.

title: The origin of the first cells
stem: Life is thought to have arisen on the early Earth from non-living matter.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline an experiment that tested whether organic molecules could form under conditions thought to exist on the early Earth.
markscheme: Miller and Urey (1950s)
mixture of gases simulating early atmosphere: methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water vapour
no free oxygen / reducing atmosphere
water boiled to produce vapour / simulated ocean
electric sparks to simulate lightning / energy source
condenser cooled gases to simulate rain
after a week amino acids / organic compounds were found in the water

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe evidence for a last universal common ancestor (LUCA) of all living organisms.
markscheme: all organisms use the same (near-)universal genetic code
all use DNA as genetic material / RNA as intermediary
all use the same 20 amino acids / L-amino acids in proteins
all use ATP as energy currency / share core metabolic pathways e.g. glycolysis
some genes are shared by all organisms e.g. ribosomal RNA / ribosomal proteins
comparison of these genes suggests LUCA lived around 4 billion years ago / near hydrothermal vents
other early forms of life became extinct, so all present life descends from LUCA

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the processes that are thought to have been needed for the origin of cells from non-living material.
markscheme: synthesis of simple organic molecules from inorganic molecules
energy sources such as lightning / UV radiation / hydrothermal vents
assembly of organic molecules into polymers (e.g. by condensation on clay / mineral surfaces)
a molecule capable of self-replication was needed
RNA could act as both a store of information and a catalyst (ribozyme) / RNA world
so RNA could replicate itself and catalyse reactions before DNA and proteins
formation of membranes / compartments to enclose molecules
fatty acids / phospholipids spontaneously form vesicles / bilayers in water
membranes allow a different internal chemistry / concentration of reactants
vesicles could grow and divide when more lipids added
development of a genetic code linking nucleic acid sequence to protein
spontaneous generation does not happen now as conditions differ / organic molecules would be consumed by existing life
parts.notes: Expect candidates to address the four key steps: monomer synthesis, polymerization, self-replication and compartmentalization.

title: Karyotypes, species and speciation
stem: Variation between species is found both in their chromosomes and in their reproductive behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how a karyotype is prepared and how it can be used.
markscheme: cells (e.g. white blood cells / fetal cells) are cultured / induced to divide
division arrested at metaphase when chromosomes are most condensed
chromosomes stained and photographed / imaged
chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs in order of size / banding / centromere position
sex chromosomes placed last
used to determine sex of individual
used to identify chromosome abnormalities e.g. trisomy 21
used to compare chromosome number / structure between species

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline why chromosome number is a characteristic feature of a species.
markscheme: members of a species have the same number of chromosomes
homologous chromosomes must pair during meiosis
hybrids between species with different chromosome numbers cannot pair chromosomes properly
so gametes are not viable / hybrids are infertile
so chromosome differences act as a barrier to interbreeding
chromosome number can change by fusion / splitting of chromosomes e.g. human chromosome 2
diploid number is twice the haploid number / chromosomes are in pairs

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how a population can split into two separate species.
markscheme: population is divided into two (or more) groups
reproductive isolation prevents gene flow between groups
geographical isolation / barrier e.g. mountain / river / sea gives allopatric speciation
behavioural / temporal isolation can occur without a barrier, giving sympatric speciation
different mutations arise in each group
environments differ so different selection pressures act
natural selection favours different alleles in each population / differential selection
allele frequencies diverge / gene pools change independently
genetic drift may also change allele frequencies, especially in small populations
over many generations the populations become so different that they cannot interbreed
even if they meet again, they no longer produce fertile offspring and are separate species
parts.notes: Award at most 5 marks if no reference to natural selection or reproductive isolation.
